It's November 2033. The district council has voted: the little square next to the new stop on Kastanienallee will be called “Ingrid-Brandt-Platz”. Susanne, who collected the signatures, reads the news item to Ludwig over the phone.

Ludwig, are you sitting down? I'll read it to you: “The district mayor declared on Wednesday evening that the decision had been taken unanimously. The little square on Kastanienallee will be called Ingrid-Brandt-Platz from the spring.”
Unanimously? Even the party that's always against everything?
Wait. “A representative of the opposition admitted that he had had reservations at first. After reading the letters from former pupils, however, he had changed his mind.”
The letters. How many were there in the end?
Two hundred and twelve. It says here: “According to the initiators, over two hundred former pupils came forward. The letters came from all over Germany, some even from Canada and Australia.”
Why does it say “hätten” and “kämen” there? I thought in the newspaper they write “haben” and “kommen” in Konjunktiv I.

Because “sie haben” and “sie kommen” in Konjunktiv I look exactly like the indicative. Then you use Konjunktiv II, so that it's clear it's someone else's statement. I've been teaching that to my pupils for thirty years. And they hate it as much as I used to.

“The mayor stressed that Ingrid Brandt had taught children for over forty years, many of them free of charge. She had been a teacher who never gave up. With this name, the intention was also to pay tribute to other teachers.”
Who never gave up. It's true. She never gave up. Not even with me.
And the last sentence: “Asked whether the family agreed, the widower, Ludwig Brandt, 85, said he had just one request: that the sign should not say «teacher», but «teacher and reader».”
They printed that? Good. That's how she would have wanted it.

Reported speech has no separate Präteritum or Plusquamperfekt: every past becomes “habe/sei + participle”.

The idea had come up in August, on a hot evening, on the bench in front of the café, and like most good ideas on Kastanienallee it had come from Elif. She had looked at the new stop, at her tree next to it, at the little paved square with the two benches and asked: “What's this square actually called?” Nobody knew. It had no name. It was simply the square in front of the stop, just as before it had been the pavement in front of the chestnut trees. “Then it should have a name,” Elif had said. “The name of someone who was important here.”

Susanne heard about it the following weekend, when she was visiting, and knew at once which name. She went back to Hanover and started writing. She wrote to Michael in Munich, who had been on the phone with all the education authorities for years. She wrote to the primary school on Kastanienallee and asked for the old class lists. She wrote a short appeal, which Katrin Krüger published in the Berliner Zeitung under the headline “Who had Mrs Brandt as a teacher?”. And then the letters started coming.

Ludwig knew nothing at first. Susanne had decided to tell him only once there was a chance of success. “He'll say no,” she had told Lena. “He'll say Ingrid wouldn't have wanted it, that she was modest, that she never wanted to be the centre of attention.” Lena had laughed. “That's all true,” she had replied. “But she would have wanted the children she taught to be heard. Tell him that.” And when Susanne told him exactly that in September, Ludwig was silent for a long time and then just said: “If you do it, then do it properly. With all the letters.”

First came five, then twenty, then so many that Susanne had to buy a big cardboard box. They came from Berlin, from Leipzig, from Munich, from a village on the Baltic. One came from Toronto, from a man who had been in Ingrid's class in 1979 and wrote that she had taught him not to be afraid of words and that today he was a professor of linguistics. One came from Sydney, from a woman who had fled with her parents through Hungary in 1988 and wrote that the only thing she had kept from her school years was a sentence of Mrs Brandt's: “Whoever reads is never completely alone.”

Ludwig read the letters too, one after another, on the October evenings, with a magnifying glass, in Ingrid's armchair. He read them slowly, sometimes only one an evening. He knew many of the names. Children he had seen holding their mothers' hands in front of the school when he came to pick Ingrid up. Children Ingrid had brought home for a meal because there was nothing at their home. Children Ingrid had talked about at dinner, with shining eyes or with worry. And now they were fifty, sixty years old, they were teachers, bus drivers, nurses, grandparents, and they wrote to her as if it had been yesterday.

Susanne read every letter. She read them in the evenings, in her kitchen in Hanover, and sometimes she had to stop because she couldn't read on. Then Peter brought her tea and read the rest aloud himself. Many letters were short, three, four sentences. Some were long, ten pages, with photos. Almost all of them told the same story, just in different words: about a teacher who believed in them when nobody else did. Who stayed after school to read with them. Who never said they were stupid. Who never gave up.

In October, Susanne brought the box to Berlin, to the meeting of the district council, together with a petition signed by fourteen hundred people. Elif had collected most of the signatures, with a list on a clipboard, at the stop, every afternoon after school, in all weathers. She had asked every passenger who got off. Most had signed. One man had asked who Ingrid Brandt was, and Elif had explained to him for ten minutes who she had been, until he missed his tram and signed anyway.

Not everyone was in favour. Mr Hartwig, a councillor from a small party that was on principle against everything that cost money, declared at the first meeting that you couldn't name every square after every teacher. There were thousands of good teachers in Berlin. Where would it end? Besides, Mrs Brandt had not been a public figure. Susanne, who was sitting in the back row, went pale. Elif, who was sitting next to her, clenched her fists. Ludwig wasn't there. He had said he couldn't sit in the same room in which strangers voted on whether his wife had been important.

Then Susanne did something she hadn't planned. She stood up, picked up the box, walked through the whole hall to the front and put it on the table in front of Mr Hartwig. “You're right,” she said calmly. “Mrs Brandt was not a public figure. She was a figure in two hundred and twelve private lives. Please read one letter. Just one. Then you can vote however you like.” The hall went very quiet. Mr Hartwig looked at the box, then at Susanne, then at the box again. He took out a letter, the one on top, and began to read.

It was, as it turned out later, the letter of a man from Marzahn, born in 1971, who had written that as a child he had stuttered, so badly that at school he couldn't get a single word out. Mrs Brandt had reportedly kept him back every day after lessons and read poems with him, slowly, word by word, for a whole year, until in the summer he was able to recite a poem by Brecht in front of the whole class without stuttering even once. Mr Hartwig read the letter to the end. Then he put it back in the box, slowly, and said nothing. The meeting was adjourned.

On the way home, on the tram, Elif was very quiet. Only when they got off at the new stop, next to her tree, did she say: “Mrs Albrecht, do you think he'll change his mind?” Susanne shrugged. “I don't know,” she said honestly. “Some people never change their minds. But some just need the right letter.” Elif thought about that. Then she said: “Then I hope it was the right one.” And Susanne, who had been a teacher for thirty years, thought that Ingrid would have loved this child.

At home, Elif told her mother everything at dinner, so excitedly that she knocked over her glass three times. Ayşe listened and smiled. Then she said something Elif hadn't expected: “You know, I had a teacher like that too. In our village, in Turkey. Her name was Mrs Yıldız. She was the first to tell me I was clever. Maybe I should write her a letter too sometime.” And the next evening, mother and daughter sat together at the kitchen table and wrote, Ayşe in Turkish, Elif in German, two letters to two teachers, only one of whom was still alive.

Two weeks later, at the decisive meeting, Mr Hartwig asked to speak before the vote. He declared that at the weekend he had read the whole box, all two hundred and twelve letters. He admitted that he had been wrong. He had thought it was about a name. But it was about something else: the question of whom a city wants to remember. He would vote for the motion. And he asked that the box not be returned, but displayed at the district museum, so that others could read the letters too. Then all fifty-one councillors voted yes. Unanimously. For the first time in four years.

The next morning a man Lena didn't know came into the café “Bei Ingrid”: around sixty-five, grey coat, a briefcase under his arm. He ordered a coffee, sat down by the window and drank it slowly. When he left, he left an envelope on the table addressed to “Mr Ludwig Brandt”. Inside was a short handwritten letter. Mr Hartwig wrote that he too had once had a teacher, in Lichtenberg, in the seventies, who believed in him when his father said he would never amount to anything. He had forgotten her. For fifty years. The letters in the box had reminded him of her. At the weekend he had looked up her name and found out that she was still alive, in a care home in Köpenick, at ninety-three. He would visit her on Sunday. For the first time. And he thanked Mr Brandt and his late wife for that.

Susanne rang Ludwig from the town hall, her voice trembling, and read him the news item that was already online an hour later. Ludwig listened without interrupting her, in Ingrid's armchair, by the window, with Fritz on his feet. When Susanne had finished, he said nothing for a long time. Then he only asked: “And the man from Marzahn? The one who stuttered? Does he know?” Susanne laughed through her tears. “He's coming to the unveiling of the sign in the spring,” she said. “He asked if he could read a poem there. By Brecht.” Ludwig closed his eyes. “Tell him yes,” he said. “Tell him Ingrid would have insisted.”
